structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase: Verizon Communications Inc. (the Company) is a holding company that, acting through its subsidiaries (together with the Company, collectively, Verizon), is one of the world’s leading providers of communications, technology, information and entertainment products and services to consumers, businesses and government entities.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: Verizon Communications Inc. is a global provider of communications, technology, information and entertainment services operating through subsidiaries, with principal offices in New York, NY. It manages two reportable segments: Verizon Consumer Group (Consumer) and Verizon Business Group (Business).

- Segment profiles and 2022 scale:
  - Consumer: $103.5B revenue (~76% of consolidated). ~115M wireless retail connections (80% postpaid, includes FWA), ~8M total broadband connections (Fios, DSL, FWA), ~3M Fios video connections. Offers wireless services/equipment, FWA, residential fixed services (Fios fiber and copper-based, LTE Home), wholesale network access to MVNOs, and non-connectivity services (device protection, cloud).
  - Business: $31.1B revenue (~23%). ~29M wireless retail postpaid connections; ~1M broadband connections (Fios, DSL, FWA). Provides wireless and wireline services: data, video, conferencing, networking, security, managed services, voice, IoT connectivity and solutions.
    - Small & Medium Business: $12.6B (~41% of Business) with wireless, Fios, voice, networking, security, and managed IT tailored to SMBs.
    - Global Enterprise: $9.7B (~31%) offering network services, advanced communications (voice/video/UCaaS/contact center), security services, core voice/data, and IoT enablement.
    - Public Sector & Other: $6.1B (~20%) serving U.S. federal, state, local government and education; includes fleet/asset/mobile resource management solutions.
    - Wholesale: $2.6B (~8%) selling data, voice (including TDM and VoIP), local dial tone and broadband to carriers; some services provided per regulatory requirements.

- Wireless services and equipment:
  - Postpaid and prepaid offerings (prepaid in Consumer only); device payment plans; broadband access via smartphones, tablets, mobile hotspots; FWA over 5G/4G LTE (~1.5M FWA connections as of year-end 2022). Consumer no longer offers new subsidized fixed-term device plans; Business continues subsidized plans.

- Distribution:
  - Direct channels: company-operated stores, sales/service centers, business direct sales, robust digital and omni-channel experience.
  - Indirect channels: exclusive agents, national retailers, convenience stores (prepaid), plus Business-focused resellers, distributors, and system integrators.

- Network and technology:
  - Intelligent Edge Network transformation to increase efficiency, virtualization, automation, and support edge computing; retirement of 3G in 2022 (removal of ~909k retail postpaid and ~237k prepaid connections).
  - 5G: deployment using millimeter wave, C-Band (covering ~189M POPs by 12/31/22), and DSS across low/mid bands; 5G supports mobile and FWA.
  - 4G LTE: primary traffic carrier; coverage ~328M POPs including Rural America partners; LTE Home Internet available.
  - Reliability/build-out: densification (small cells, in-building, DAS), spectrum additions, advanced tech, redundant backbone, extensive backup power, and portable generators; domestic and international roaming.
  - Fios: PON-based 100% fiber network supporting growing residential bandwidth needs; expanding use in Business.
  - Global IP: large global fiber network (long-haul, metro, submarine) serving customers in 180+ countries; deploying packet optical transport.
  - Spectrum: extensive low/mid-band holdings (cellular, PCS, 700 MHz C-Block, AWS, C-Band, CBRS, LAA) and millimeter wave (28, 37/39 GHz). Uses DSS to operate 4G and 5G concurrently; pursues spectrum swaps/purchases to optimize contiguity and capacity.

- Competitive environment and trends:
  - Intense competition across wireless and wireline from national and regional carriers (e.g., AT&T, T-Mobile), cable MVNOs (e.g., Comcast, Charter), OTT/tech firms (e.g., Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple, Meta), satellite (LEO) and fixed wireless entrants. Drivers include 5G deployment, promotions, bundled content, spectrum availability, and government incentives.
  - Key competitive factors: network reliability/speed/coverage, pricing and device promotions, customer service, product differentiation and rapid innovation, and breadth/quality of sales and distribution.

- Regulatory landscape:
  - FCC is primary federal regulator; some services also face state/local oversight. Key areas include spectrum licensing/renewal, open access obligations, E911, roaming, build-out, and zoning/land use for towers.
  - Broadband currently treated as an information service (light-touch), though utility-style regulation could return; some states pursuing their own rules; Verizon affirms open internet commitment.
  - Wireline voice: legacy services as common carrier; VoIP subject to certain rules though classification unresolved; state commissions regulate intrastate matters with varying oversight.
  - Video: facilities-based multichannel video regulated like cable; franchise requirements and ongoing obligations.
  - Privacy/data security: subject to U.S. federal (FCC/FTC), state (e.g., CCPA), and international (e.g., GDPR) regimes with increasing global scrutiny and penalties.
  - Public safety/cybersecurity: emergency communications, alerts, potential added cybersecurity regulation; restrictions on certain foreign equipment vendors (Verizon notes none in its networks); disaster-related continuity rules (e.g., disaster roaming, backup power).
  - Intercarrier compensation and network access: FCC regulates certain interconnection, access rates, and business data services; Verizon is both a buyer and seller.

- Human capital:
  - ~117,100 FTE employees (89% U.S.) as of 12/31/22. Focus on attracting, developing, and engaging diverse talent; robust training, tuition assistance, and upskilling. Diversity metrics provided for gender and U.S. race/ethnicity; women and people of color representation in senior leadership noted.
  - Labor relations: ~22.5% unionized (CWA and IBEW); CBAs in Mid-Atlantic/Northeast extend through August 1, 2026; engagement with unions and works councils.

- Intellectual property:
  - Extensive patents, trademarks, copyrights, and domain names; active filing, protection, and licensing programs. Potential exposure to third-party IP claims noted but loss/expiration not expected to be materially adverse.

- Corporate information and disclosures:
  - Executive officers referenced in Part III, Item 10.
  - Investor website provides SEC filings, financial and ESG information; website references not incorporated by reference.

- Forward-looking statements and risks:
  - Safe harbor statement included; outlines multiple risk factors that could cause actual results to differ, including competition, technology deployment (notably 5G), economic conditions (including inflation), cybersecurity and natural disasters, supply chain/geopolitics, labor, regulatory changes, indebtedness, litigation, credit markets, benefits costs, tax and accounting changes.
  - Item 1A Risk Factors begins with detailed discussion of economic and strategic risks, highlighting intense competition and the need to keep pace with technology and consumer demand.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: The following discussion of "Risk Factors" identifies factors that may adversely affect our business, operations, financial condition or future performance.
structure.summary:
- Extract from Verizon’s 2022 Form 10-K, Item 1A: Risk Factors, outlining material risks that could adversely affect business, operations, financial condition, and performance, with emphasis on forward-looking uncertainties.
- Economic and strategic risks:
  - Intense industry competition across wireless, cable, internet, satellite, and tech/app ecosystems, pressuring pricing and margins and risking impairment if unit performance declines.
  - Rapid technology change; execution risks in new products/services and timely 5G deployment (equipment/spectrum availability, costs, regulation); challenges and potential constraints in phasing out legacy technologies.
  - Macroeconomic headwinds (recession, inflation) reducing demand, increasing bad debt, and raising operating costs (energy, transport, labor) and interest expense; 2022 inflation impacted earnings and guidance, with pressures expected to continue.
- Operational risks:
  - Cybersecurity threats (malware, DDoS, ransomware, social engineering) affecting Verizon and its suppliers/vendors, with potential for service disruption, data compromise, reputational harm, litigation, and increased security costs; added exposure from IoT/telematics and security businesses.
  - Natural disasters, extreme weather, and geopolitical events (war/terrorism) damaging infrastructure; climate change increasing severity/frequency of events; redundancy and disaster recovery may be insufficient; supplier infrastructure also vulnerable.
  - Public health crises (e.g., COVID-19) impacting customer usage and payment behavior, operations, supply chains, financing, and regulatory risks; prior adverse impacts on revenue, costs, and EPS noted.
  - Dependence on key suppliers and vendors (including single/limited-source components and network equipment); global supply chain disruptions (geopolitical, health, climate) can delay products/services, raise costs, and hinder network upgrades; switching suppliers is costly and slow.
  - Labor relations: significant unionized workforce; renegotiations may increase costs or cause work stoppages; potential impacts from increased union density.
- Regulatory and legal risks:
  - Extensive U.S. and international regulation (FCC and other authorities); licensing requirements and uncertainty of proceedings; new/changed rules may raise costs, limit operations, or constrain network management and service strategies.
  - Privacy/data protection (CCPA, GDPR, emerging state/global laws) with significant penalties and compliance burdens.
  - Broadband regulation and net neutrality: prior Title II reclassification in 2015, repeal in 2017, potential federal/state changes creating uncertainty and compliance complexity.
  - “Open access” obligations on certain spectrum and potential overlapping federal/state/local rules increasing deployment costs.
  - Climate-related policy (GHG regulation, carbon pricing/taxes) potentially raising energy and fleet fuel costs.
  - Substantial litigation exposure (shareholder, patent, wage/hour, commercial, personal injury, environmental, marketing/billing practices; wireless health effects claims) with significant defense and settlement risks.
- Financial risks:
  - High leverage (approx. $130.6B unsecured and $20.0B secured debt as of 12/31/22) limiting financial flexibility, increasing vulnerability to downturns, and exposing to interest rate risk; revolver capacity noted.
  - Adverse credit market conditions (rates, FX, collateral needs) and potential ratings downgrades could raise borrowing costs and constrain access; securitization dependent on eligible asset origination; systemic financial instability could affect financing access.
  - Rising costs for pensions and healthcare benefits (large employee/retiree base) driven by healthcare inflation, investment returns, discount rate/mortality changes, potentially reducing profitability and increasing funding needs.
  - Additional overarching risks noted: changes in tax laws/treaties or interpretations, and changes in accounting rules/assumptions (including SEC requirements) that could affect earnings.
- Item 1B: Unresolved Staff Comments — none.

- Mentions potential litigation related to radio frequency transmitters that could lead to significant defense costs and possible awards or settlements.
- Outlines financial risks tied to Verizon’s leverage: as of December 31, 2022, about $130.6B in unsecured debt, $20.0B in secured debt, and $9.4B of unused revolver capacity.

- Item 2 – Properties: Verizon’s properties are diverse and not easily summarized by location. Gross investment in property, plant and equipment totaled approximately $308 billion at December 31, 2022 (vs. $290 billion at December 31, 2021), before accumulated depreciation. Composition at year-end 2022 (and 2021): Network equipment 77.2% (76.9%); Land, buildings and building equipment 11.7% (11.7%); Furniture and other 11.1% (11.4%). Network equipment includes cable and support structures, wireless plant, switching equipment, network software, transmission equipment and related facilities. Land/buildings cover network and administrative facilities; most switching centers are owned due to criticality and relocation costs. Facilities across the U.S. include offices, customer care, retail, garages, switching centers, cell sites and data centers. Furniture/other includes telephone equipment, furniture, IT/office equipment, vehicles, construction in process and leasehold improvements.

- Item 3 – Legal Proceedings: Verizon is involved in routine litigation and regulatory matters at state and federal levels; as of the report date, no proceedings require disclosure as material. The company is not subject to environmental proceedings likely to result in monetary sanctions of $1 million or more. Litigation risks are discussed in Item 1A Risk Factors.

- Item 4 – Mine Safety Disclosures: None.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
Verizon Communications Inc. (the Company) is a holding company that, acting through its subsidiaries (together with the 
Company, collectively, Verizon), is one of the world’s leading providers of communications, technology, information and 
entertainment products and services to consumers, businesses and government entities.
structure.summary:
- Executive overview of Verizon’s business, strategy, and network leadership, emphasizing 2022 priorities: rapid C-Band deployment, 5G expansion, Intelligent Edge Network, fiber investment, and balancing customer growth with profitability.
- 2022 financial highlights: operating revenues, operating income, net income, cash flows from operations, and capital expenditures, noting 2022 as a peak capex year due to C-Band.
- Reportable segments and revenue mix: Verizon Consumer Group, Verizon Business Group, and Corporate & Other (with mix shift vs. 2021 and the impact of the 2021 Verizon Media divestiture).
- Global Network and Technology: continued 4G densification, nationwide 5G build, C-Band coverage reaching ~189M POPs by year-end 2022, DSS for seamless 4G/5G, fiber build, and migration to Intelligent Edge Network for efficiency and new edge opportunities.
- Consolidated results of operations:
  - Revenues: increase driven by Consumer and Business, offset by decline in Corporate & Other following Verizon Media sale.
  - Expenses: detail on cost of services (lower media-related costs; higher access and rent), higher cost of wireless equipment (TracFone inclusion, higher volumes, premium mix), higher SG&A (credit losses tied to 36‑month plans, TracFone, prior-year media gain), and higher D&A (C-Band/intangibles).
  - Other income (expense): pension/postretirement remeasurement credits and lower debt extinguishment losses vs. 2021.
  - Interest expense: slight increase; higher capitalized interest on C-Band.
  - Provision for income taxes: stable effective rate; lower tax provision on lower pre-tax income.
  - Non-GAAP metrics: Consolidated EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA with reconciliations and explanation of special items.
- Segment performance and operating metrics:
  - Consumer: services (postpaid, prepaid/TracFone, FWA, Fios), revenue up 8.6% (service and equipment growth; lower “Other” from device protection mix), operating stats (connections, churn, ARPA up, strong broadband/FWA adds), expense drivers (access costs, tower rents, equipment volumes/mix, higher credit losses and advertising), margins and EBITDA trends.
  - Business: customer groups (SMB, Global Enterprise, Public Sector & Other, Wholesale); flat total revenue with SMB growth offset by declines in Enterprise/Public Sector/Wholesale; strong wireless postpaid adds (phones and FWA), broadband growth; expense changes and margin compression.
- Special items: amortization of acquisition intangibles, severance/pension credits, early debt redemption costs, gains/losses on dispositions and spectrum transactions, and how these are treated in Adjusted EBITDA.
- Operating environment and trends: competitive dynamics across wireless and wireline; pricing/promotions and device incentives; 5G use cases and ecosystem development; FWA and IoT growth; secular declines in legacy wireline; increasing competition from cable MVNOs and LEO satellite entrants; inflationary pressures on costs and consumer price sensitivity.
- 2023 outlook commentary: expected drivers of connections (FWA, devices, wearables), revenue (mix shift to higher access plans, FWA growth, pricing actions), continued Fios broadband growth vs. video pressure; Business wireless growth and ongoing wireline secular headwinds; margin focus and cost efficiency (Global Services); lower capex post C-Band build phase; cash flow and capital allocation priorities.
- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Cash position and funding sources (operations, debt markets, ABS, credit facilities).
  - 2023 capex guidance ($18.25–$19.25B, including final $1.75B of accelerated C-Band program).
  - Contractual obligations: debt and interest, lease commitments, purchase obligations, C-Band clearing commitments, pension/postretirement payments, and tax contingencies.
  - Cash flows: operating (lower on higher device receivables and earnings), investing (capex and C-Band clearing/incentive payments), financing (debt activity, dividends), and free cash flow reconciliation.
- Capital structure and financing:
  - Total debt levels and effective interest rates; mix of fixed/variable; foreign-denominated debt with cross-currency swaps.
  - Asset-backed debt program secured by device receivables, restricted cash mechanics, and non-recourse structure.
  - Credit facilities (unused $9.5B revolver; export credit facilities draws), derivatives usage and collateral postings.
- Capital allocation and shareholder returns: dividend policy and 2022 increase (16th consecutive year); authorized share repurchase program (no 2022/2021 activity); stable credit ratings and covenant compliance.
- Employee benefit plans: funding status, LDI strategy, expected 2023 contributions (qualified pension and OPEB).
- Critical accounting estimates: impairment testing for wireless licenses (Greenfield approach; no impairment) and goodwill (Consumer qualitative pass; Business quantitative pass with ~8% headroom and elevated future risk), pension/OPEB assumptions and sensitivities, income tax uncertainties, PP&E useful life sensitivity, and accounts receivable credit loss methodology and sensitivity.
- Acquisitions and divestitures:
  - TracFone acquisition (consideration mix, contingent consideration and 2022 fair value changes/cash payments).
  - Bluegrass Cellular acquisition (2021).
  - Verizon Media sale to Apollo (2021 gain and proceeds).
  - Spectrum transactions: Auction 107 (C-Band) payments and ongoing clearing/incentive obligations; early clearing agreements in 2022; Auction 103 (mmWave) context.
- Market risk disclosures: interest rate and FX exposures, hedging strategy (ISDA/CSA), and policy limits; not using derivatives for trading.

- TracFone contingent consideration: Initial fair value $560M (Level 3), tied to two-year revenue/operational earn-out. 2022 payments of $188M (financing cash flows); further payments expected through 2024. Fair value at 12/31/22 was $317M; $57M gain from fair value adjustments recorded in SG&A.

- Bluegrass Cellular acquisition: Closed March 2021; cash consideration approximately $412M, net of cash acquired.

- Verizon Media divestiture: Agreement with an Apollo affiliate to sell Verizon Media for $4.3B cash, $750M preferred LP units, and 10% common LP units. Closed 9/1/21 with recognized values of $4.3B cash, $496M preferred, $124M common; recorded pre-tax (and after-tax) gain of ~$1.0B in 2021 SG&A; incurred $346M of disposition-related costs.

- Other transactions: 2022 non-strategic divestiture and other activity produced an insignificant pre-tax net gain. In Dec 2021, sale of an investment generated a $131M pre-tax gain recorded in Equity in earnings of unconsolidated businesses.

- Market risk management: Exposure to interest rate, FX, investment/equity/commodity prices, and corporate tax rate changes. Uses derivatives (cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps/caps, forward-starting swaps, treasury locks, FX forwards) for risk management, not trading. Targets an optimized fixed/variable debt mix; does not fully eliminate earnings/cash flow volatility.

- Derivative counterparties and collateral: ISDA/CSA agreements with major financial institutions; rating-based collateral thresholds. At 12/31/22, posted $2.3B collateral (recorded as Prepaid expenses and other); no collateral held. At 12/31/21, held $0.1B and posted an insignificant amount. Counterparty nonperformance risk considered remote.

- Interest rate risk profile: About 74% of total debt at fixed rates (including swaps) at 12/31/22. A 100 bps move changes annual interest expense by ~+$/-420M. LIBOR transition: USD LIBOR ceases after 6/30/23; shift to SOFR since 2021; impact not expected to be significant.

- Fair value sensitivity of long-term debt and related derivatives:
  - 12/31/22 fair value $143.6B; with +100 bps $136.2B; with -100 bps $152.4B.
  - 12/31/21 fair value $169.2B; with +100 bps $156.1B; with -100 bps $184.5B.

- Interest rate swaps: Fair value hedges (receive fixed, pay variable). At 12/31/22, liability fair value $4.6B; notional $26.1B. At 12/31/21, asset $473M and liability $666M; notional $19.8B. 2022 liability increase driven by rate changes.

- Forward-starting interest rate swaps: Cash flow hedges. No outstanding notional or fair value at 12/31/22; at 12/31/21, $1.0B notional and $302M liability.

- Treasury rate locks: No outstanding positions at 12/31/22 or 12/31/21.

- Foreign currency translation: Local currency functional for foreign ops; translation adjustments in AOCI; transaction gains/losses in income statement. Primary translation exposure to GBP, EUR, AUD.

- Cross-currency swaps: Used to convert GBP/EUR/CHF/CAD/AUD cash flows to USD and fix USD payments; de-designated from cash flow hedges and re-designated as fair value hedges on 3/31/22. At 12/31/22: asset $305M, liability $3.6B, notional $35.0B. At 12/31/21: asset $589M, liability $1.6B, notional $32.5B.

- FX forwards: Economic hedges (no hedge accounting) for GBP and EUR exposures of non-functional currency balances. Fair values insignificant; notional $920M at 12/31/22 ($932M at 12/31/21).

- Use of estimates: preparation under U.S. GAAP with significant estimates for credit losses, asset recoverability (intangibles, PP&E), lease discount rates, fair value (including financial instruments, goodwill, spectrum, intangibles), tax uncertainties and valuation allowances, pension/postretirement obligations, contingencies, and business combinations; consideration of forward-looking factors such as COVID-19.
- Revenue recognition: primary revenues accounted for under ASC 606 from telecommunications and related services and equipment sales; non-ASC 606 revenues from leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on agent-sold device financing.
- Service revenue: wireless recognized over time using output methods (usage/time); monthly services typically billed in advance creating contract liabilities; overage usage recognized when incurred. Wireline fixed fees billed in advance and recognized over the enforceable term; usage-based services billed in arrears and recognized as used.
- Equipment revenue: recognized upon delivery/acceptance (transfer of control); device offerings via fixed-term contracts (discounted/zero-cost devices with service commitment) or device payment plans (interest-free installments, typically 36 months, with month-to-month service). Promotional billing credits included in transaction price and allocated based on relative standalone selling prices and recognized when earned.
- Financing component: present in fixed-term and device payment plans due to timing differences; assessed as not significant for direct-channel contracts, thus not accounted for separately; interest on certain indirect-channel financings addressed elsewhere.
- Wireless contract accounting: allocation of transaction price between service and equipment based on standalone selling prices (device at retail price excluding subsidies; service at month-to-month price without fixed term or device purchase). Consideration of legally enforceable rights/obligations (e.g., early termination penalties, cessation of credits) in determining service term and transaction price. Trade-in upgrade rights treated as guarantee obligations measured at fair value.

nodes.title: Nature of Products and Services
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.6 Nature of Products and Services
nodes.start_phrase: We offer wireless services through a variety of plans on a postpaid or prepaid basis.
nodes.summary:
- Describes revenue streams outside ASC 606, including leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on equipment financed via authorized agents.
- Explains revenue recognition for wireless services (postpaid/prepaid) using an output method; monthly billing in advance creates contract liabilities; overage charges treated as options recognized when exercised.
- Details wireline service billing (fixed fees billed in advance; usage-based billed in arrears) with revenue recognized over the enforceable term as services are consumed.
- Outlines equipment revenue recognition at delivery and two device offerings: fixed-term subsidized plans and 36‑month device payment plans; billing credits included in transaction price; financing components assessed and generally not significant in direct channel.
- Provides wireless contract accounting: allocation of transaction price between service and equipment using standalone selling prices (retail device price and month‑to‑month service price); consideration of legally enforceable rights (e.g., early termination penalties, cessation of credits) affecting service term and transaction price.
- Accounts for device upgrade promotions with trade‑in rights as guarantee liabilities reducing equipment revenue (with reported balances for 2022 and 2021).
- Notes creation of contract assets for subsidized devices and contract liabilities for billing credits; handles returns, reseller credits, and incentives as variable consideration updated each reporting period.
- Covers wireline contracts: allocation to performance obligations based on standalone prices; recognition typically over the same time period; performance‑based credits for Business customers treated as variable consideration.
- Describes principal vs. agent assessments for third‑party offerings based on control indicators (fulfillment responsibility, risk of loss, pricing discretion).
- Summarizes “Other” revenues: advertising (display, search, subscriptions) recognition patterns; generally principal on advertising platforms; mentions sale of Verizon Media on September 1, 2021; telematics revenues recognized over time via subscriptions.
- States taxes collected on behalf of authorities are reported net.
- Notes maintenance and repair costs are expensed to Cost of services as incurred.

nodes.title: Maintenance and Repairs
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.7 Maintenance and Repairs
nodes.start_phrase: We charge the cost of maintenance and repairs, including the cost of replacing minor items not constituting substantial betterments, principally to Cost of services as these costs are incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue recognition and consideration adjustments:
  - Device sales include a guarantee liability that reduces recognized revenue; liability was $54 million at December 31, 2022 and $77 million at December 31, 2021. The guarantee is outside Topic 606; the remaining transaction price is allocated to performance obligations.
  - Fixed-term wireless plans with subsidized devices create contract assets (equipment revenue recognized in excess of billings).
  - Device payment plan billing credits are treated as consideration payable, creating contract liabilities.
  - Rights of return and reseller credits/incentives are treated as variable consideration; estimates are set at inception and updated each reporting period.

- Wireline contracts:
  - Consideration for bundled services is allocated to performance obligations based on standalone selling prices; services are generally recognized over time.
  - Judgment is applied to assess legally enforceable rights/obligations (e.g., early termination penalties) that affect service term, transaction price, and disclosures.
  - Performance-based credits/incentives for Business customers are variable consideration.

- Wireless and Wireline with third-party providers:
  - Principal-versus-agent assessment based on control indicators (primary responsibility for fulfillment, risk of loss, pricing discretion).

- Other revenues:
  - Advertising: display and search ad revenue recognized as ads are delivered; subscription advertising revenue recognized over time. Typically reported on a gross (principal) basis due to control via proprietary ad platforms. Verizon Media was sold on September 1, 2021.
  - Telematics services: subscription-based, revenue recognized over time.
  - Taxes collected from customers are reported on a net basis.

- Maintenance and repairs:
  - Routine maintenance and minor replacements are expensed to Cost of services as incurred.

nodes.title: Advertising Costs

nodes.title: Investments in Debt and Equity Securities
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.11 Investments in Debt and Equity Securities

nodes.title: Allowance for Credit Losses
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.12 Allowance for Credit Losses
nodes.start_phrase: Accounts receivable are recorded at amortized cost less an allowance for credit losses that are not expected to be recovered.
nodes.summary:
- Advertising costs: Expensed to Selling, general and administrative (SG&A) when incurred; includes promotional and sponsorship spend.

- Cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash: Cash equivalents are highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less, recorded at cost approximating fair value (e.g., money market funds). Restricted cash arises from asset-backed debt collections placed in segregated accounts and is reported in Prepaid expenses and other and Other assets. Balances at December 31:

  - 2021: Cash and cash equivalents $2,921M; Restricted cash—Prepaid expenses and other $1,094M; Restricted cash—Other assets $146M; Total $4,161M.
- Investments in debt and equity securities: Equity securities measured at fair value unless the measurement alternative (cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes) is elected for securities without readily determinable fair values. - Allowance for credit losses: Receivables recorded at amortized cost less an allowance recognized at inception and reassessed quarterly, based on historical losses, customer credit quality, aging, macroeconomic factors (including COVID-19), and forward-looking expectations. Device payment plan receivables are pooled by “new” (<210 days) and “existing” (≥210 days) customers; allowances determined via a proprietary loss model using customer credit scores by vintage. Wireless service receivables are pooled as one group; wireline is pooled by consumer, SMB, global enterprise, public sector, and wholesale. - Inventories: Wireless and wireline equipment held for sale, carried at lower of cost (average cost or FIFO) or net realizable value.

Gains/losses on disposals recognized in SG&A. Network software is capitalized within PP&E; interest on network asset construction is capitalized, reducing interest expense and depreciated with the asset.
- Computer software and cloud computing: Capitalize internal-use network and non-network software and defer qualifying cloud computing implementation costs with terms >1 year; expense planning, maintenance, and training. Capitalize interest on software development. Amortize non-network internal-use software straight-line over 7 years (reported in Other intangible assets, net). Cloud implementation costs deferred in Prepaid expenses and other until ready for intended use; deferred amounts subject to impairment.
- Goodwill and other intangible assets: Goodwill tested for impairment annually in Q4 or when indicators arise. nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.13 Inventories
nodes.start_phrase: Inventory consists of wireless and wireline equipment held for sale, which is carried at the lower of cost (determined principally on either an average cost or first-in, first-out basis) or net realizable value.

Allowance for wireless, consumer, and SMB based on a 12-month rolling average of write-offs multiplied by average account life, adjusted for current/future conditions. For global enterprise, public sector, and wholesale, allowances reflect historical write-offs and specific customer credit risk.

Disposals remove cost/accumulated depreciation with gains/losses in SG&A. Network software is capitalized within PP&E and depreciated; interest on network-related assets is capitalized and reduces interest expense.
- Computer software and cloud computing: Capitalize internal-use network and non-network software with useful life >1 year; capitalize only enhancements adding significant functionality; expense planning, maintenance, and training. Capitalize interest on development. Amortize capitalized non-network software over 7 years (reported in Other intangible assets, net). Defer eligible cloud implementation costs during application-development stage (recorded in Prepaid expense and other) until ready for use. Capitalized software and deferred cloud costs are subject to impairment testing.
- Goodwill and other intangibles: Goodwill equals excess purchase price over fair value of net assets acquired. Impairment testing performed annually in Q4 or as needed; company may perform a qualitative screen or a quantitative test (performed at least every three years). nodes.title: Plant and Depreciation
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.14 Plant and Depreciation

- Credit losses on receivables: Wireless service receivables are monitored as one pool; wireline receivables are pooled by customer group (consumer, small and medium business, global enterprise, public sector, wholesale). Allowances for wireless, consumer, and SMB are based on a 12‑month rolling average write‑offs multiplied by average account life from billing to write‑off, adjusted for current and expected conditions via management’s qualitative factors. - Goodwill: Defined as excess purchase price over fair value of net assets acquired. nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.16.1 Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill is the excess of the acquisition cost of businesses over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired.
nodes.summary:
- Accounts receivable and credit losses: Wireless service receivables are monitored as one pool; wireline receivables are pooled by consumer, small and medium business, global enterprise, public sector, and wholesale. Allowances for wireless and wireline consumer/SMB are based on a 12‑month rolling average of write-offs multiplied by the average billing-to-write-off lifecycle, adjusted for current and expected conditions. Global enterprise, public sector, and wholesale allowances consider historical write-offs and individual customer credit risk.
- Inventories: Wireless and wireline equipment held for sale carried at lower of cost (average cost or FIFO) or net realizable value.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost and depreciated on a straight-line basis. Leasehold improvements are amortized over the shorter of useful life or remaining lease term. Disposals’ gains/losses recognized in SG&A. Network software is capitalized within PP&E. Interest on acquisition/construction of network assets is capitalized, reduces interest expense, and is depreciated with the asset.
- Software and cloud computing: Capitalize internal-use network and non-network software with useful life >1 year; defer implementation costs of qualifying cloud computing arrangements. Capitalize additions only if they add significant functionality; expense planning, maintenance, and training. Capitalize interest during software development. Non-network internal-use software is amortized straight-line over 7 years and presented in Other intangible assets, net. Cloud implementation costs are deferred in Prepaid expense and other until ready for use. Deferred software/cloud costs are subject to impairment; see Note 4.
- Goodwill: Tested annually in Q4 or more frequently if indicators arise. Option to perform a qualitative screen; quantitative testing performed at least every three years. Quantitative test compares reporting unit fair value (market multiples and discounted cash flows; Level 3) to carrying value; discount rate reflects WACC; impairment limited to the unit’s goodwill balance. Strategic five-year plans updated annually; see Note 4.
- Indefinite-lived intangibles (wireless licenses): Treated as indefinite-lived due to routine FCC renewals and lack of limiting factors; aggregated as a single unit of accounting. Annual or triggered impairment testing with option for qualitative screen; quantitative testing performed at least every three years using the Greenfield (income/DCF) approach. Capitalize interest during qualifying activities until ready for intended use. FCC auction deposits recorded in Other assets and as investing cash flows until licenses are received.
- Intangibles subject to amortization and long-lived assets: Primarily customer lists and non-network internal-use software; amortized over estimated useful lives. Impairment testing upon indicators via recoverability (undiscounted cash flows) then fair value if needed. Useful lives reassessed annually.
- Additional references: Fair value measurements are Level 3 where noted; cross-references to Note 4 for goodwill and software details.

nodes.title: Intangible Assets Not Subject to Amortization
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.16.2 Intangible Assets Not Subject to Amortization
nodes.start_phrase: A significant portion of our intangible assets are wireless licenses that provide our wireless operations with the exclusive right to utilize designated radio frequency spectrum to provide wireless communication services.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing methodology:
  - Fair value of reporting units measured using Level 3 inputs via a combination of market (comparative multiples) and income (discounted cash flow with terminal value) approaches.
  - Discount rate based on estimated weighted-average cost of capital reflecting a market participant view.
  - Impairment recognized when carrying value exceeds fair value, limited to the reporting unit’s goodwill balance.
  - Annual fourth-quarter strategic plan update informs assumptions (economy, growth, regulatory outlook); see Note 4.

- Indefinite-lived intangible assets (wireless licenses):
  - Treated as indefinite-lived due to routine, low-cost FCC renewals and absence of limiting factors; aggregated into a single unit of accounting given integrated nationwide use.
  - Annual impairment assessment (more frequent if indicators), with option for qualitative screen; company policy to perform a quantitative test at least every three years.
  - Qualitative factors include enterprise value of the wireless business, macro conditions (interest/discount rates), industry trends, performance, and prior test results.
  - Quantitative test uses the Greenfield approach (income-based DCF for a hypothetical startup owning only the licenses); impairment recorded if fair value is below carrying amount.
  - Capitalization of interest during qualifying activities to ready licenses; capitalization ends when substantially complete or development stops.
  - FCC auction deposits recorded in Other assets until licenses are received and classified in investing cash flows.

- Intangible assets subject to amortization and other long-lived assets:
  - Primarily customer lists and non-network internal-use software; amortized over estimated useful lives.
  - Impairment review upon triggering events: recoverability test via undiscounted cash flows at the asset-group level, followed by fair value measurement and impairment if necessary.
  - Annual re-evaluation of useful lives for potential revisions.

nodes.title: Intangible Assets Subject to Amortization and Long-Lived Assets
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.16.3 Intangible Assets Subject to Amortization and Long-Lived Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Our intangible assets that do not have indefinite lives (primarily customer lists and non-network internal-use software) are amortized over their estimated useful lives.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing: Annual evaluation using both market (comparative multiples) and income (discounted cash flow) approaches with Level 3 inputs; discount rate based on weighted-average cost of capital; impairment recognized if carrying value exceeds fair value, capped at the goodwill balance; informed by an annual fourth-quarter five-year strategic planning process. Reference to Note 4 for details.

- Indefinite-lived intangible assets (wireless licenses): Treated as indefinite-lived due to routine FCC renewals and lack of limiting factors; aggregated into a single unit of accounting for the nationwide network; impairment tested annually or upon indicators, with a policy to perform a quantitative test at least every three years; qualitative assessment considers macro, industry, performance, and prior results; quantitative valuation uses the Greenfield (income-based DCF) approach; impairment recognized if fair value is below carrying amount; capitalization of interest during qualifying activities; FCC auction deposits recorded in Other assets and as investing cash flows. Reference to Note 4.

- Intangible assets subject to amortization and other long-lived assets: Amortized over estimated useful lives (e.g., customer lists, internal-use software); impairment testing triggered by indicators using a two-step process (undiscounted cash flow recoverability test, then fair value measurement if not recoverable); annual reassessment of useful lives. Reference to Note 4 for carrying amounts and useful lives.

- Leases (ASC 842): Recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for operating and finance leases at commencement using an incremental borrowing rate derived via a portfolio approach (unsecured rate adjusted to collateralized, updated quarterly); non-lease and lease components combined for lessee accounting across most asset classes; for certain lessor arrangements, lease and non-lease components combined and accounted for under Topic 606 when service is predominant; operating lease expense recognized straight-line; variable lease payments expensed as incurred; short-term leases (≤12 months) not capitalized; finance lease ROU assets amortized straight-line and interest recognized via effective interest method. Reference to Note 6.

- Fair value measurements: Definition as exit price; three-level hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs); classification based on the lowest significant input; significant judgment may be required.

- Income taxes: Effective tax rate driven by pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws, and planning; deferred taxes recognized for temporary differences and remeasured annually for expected rates; valuation allowances recorded when realization is not more likely than not.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.17 Leases
nodes.start_phrase: We lease network equipment including towers, distributed antenna systems, small cells, real estate, connectivity mediums which include dark fiber, equipment, and other various types of assets for use in our operations under both operating and finance leases.
nodes.summary:
- References to Note 4 for details on goodwill, wireless licenses, and other intangible assets, including carrying amounts, major components, and average useful lives.
- Lease accounting under ASC 842:
  - Identification of lease arrangements at inception and classification/measurement at commencement.
  - Recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for operating and finance leases; present value measured using an incremental borrowing rate determined via a portfolio approach, adjusted from unsecured to approximate a collateralized rate and updated quarterly.
  - Lessee policy to combine lease and non-lease components; lessor policy to combine lease and service components under Topic 606 when service is predominant.
  - Operating leases: straight-line rent expense; variable payments (e.g., taxes, CAM, utilities) expensed as incurred; short-term leases (12 months or less) not recognized on the balance sheet.
  - Finance leases: straight-line amortization of right-of-use assets in depreciation and amortization; interest expense recognized via the effective interest method.
  - Cross-reference to Note 6 for detailed lease disclosures under ASU 2016-02 (Topic 842).
- Fair value measurements:
  - Fair value defined as exit price in an orderly transaction.
  - Use of a three-level hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs).
  - Classification based on the lowest significant input, with judgment affecting valuation and hierarchy placement.
- Income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate driven by pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws/regulations, and tax planning across jurisdictions.
  - Deferred taxes recognized for temporary differences and remeasured annually at enacted rates for expected periods of realization/settlement.
  - Valuation allowances recorded to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts more likely than not to be realized.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.18 Fair Value Measurements
nodes.start_phrase: Fair value of financial and non-financial assets and liabilities is defined as an exit price, representing the amount that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants.
nodes.summary:
- References to Note 4 for details on goodwill, wireless licenses, other intangible assets, and the major components and average useful lives of acquired intangibles.
- Lease accounting under ASC 842:
  - Verizon leases network equipment (towers, DAS, small cells), real estate, connectivity assets (e.g., dark fiber), and other equipment under operating and finance leases.
  - At lease inception, determines whether an arrangement contains a lease, then recognizes right-of-use assets and lease liabilities measured using an incremental borrowing rate derived from unsecured rates adjusted to a collateralized basis and updated quarterly.
  - Lessee practical expedient to combine lease and non-lease components; lessor treatment of customer-premise equipment arrangements by combining lease and service components under ASC 606 when service is predominant.
  - Operating lease expense recognized straight-line in Cost of services or SG&A; variable payments (taxes, CAM, utilities) expensed as incurred; short-term leases (12 months or less) kept off-balance sheet.
  - Finance leases: ROU asset amortized straight-line in depreciation and amortization; interest recognized via effective interest method in interest expense.
  - Reference to Note 6 for additional ASC 842 disclosures.
- Fair value measurements:
  - Fair value defined as exit price; uses a three-level input hierarchy (Level 1 quoted prices, Level 2 observable inputs, Level 3 unobservable inputs).
  - Classification based on the lowest significant input; valuation requires judgment affecting hierarchy placement.
- Income taxes:
  - Effective tax rate driven by pre-tax income, statutory rates, laws/regulations, and tax planning across jurisdictions.
  - Deferred taxes recorded for temporary differences and remeasured annually at enacted rates; valuation allowances recorded when realization is not more likely than not.

nodes.title: Income Taxes
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.19 Income Taxes
nodes.start_phrase: Our effective tax rate is based on pre-tax income, statutory tax rates, tax laws and regulations and tax planning strategies available to us in the various jurisdictions in which we operate.
nodes.summary:
- References to Note 4 for goodwill, wireless licenses, and other intangibles, including components and useful lives.
- Lease accounting under ASC 842: identification and classification at commencement; recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for operating and finance leases using an incremental borrowing rate set via a portfolio, collateralized-rate approach updated quarterly.
- Policy to combine lease and non-lease components as a single component for most lessee asset classes; as lessor, combine lease and service components under Topic 606 when service is predominant.
- Expense recognition: straight-line rent for operating leases; variable lease payments expensed as incurred; short-term leases (12 months or less) not capitalized; finance lease amortization in depreciation and interest via effective interest method. Cross-reference to Note 6.
- Fair value measurement framework: exit price notion; three-level hierarchy (Levels 1–3); classification by the lowest significant input; reliance on judgment in categorization.
- Income tax policies: effective tax rate drivers; deferred tax recognition and remeasurement; valuation allowances; two-step ASC 740 process for uncertain tax positions (recognition and measurement) and resulting balance sheet impacts; emphasis on management judgment.
- Stock-based compensation measured and expensed at estimated fair value (see Note 10).
- Foreign currency: local currency as functional for foreign ops; translation to USD (average rates for income statement, end-of-period for balance sheet); translation adjustments to AOCI; transaction gains/losses to Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: accrual of pension/postretirement service and interest cost; amortization of prior service cost; expected return on assets; actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net at year-end measurement; funded status recognized on the balance sheet with related amounts in AOCI; Verizon management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy (see Note 11).
- Derivative instruments: used for FX and interest rate risk (cross currency swaps, interest rate swaps, caps, swaptions, forwards, etc.); not for trading; measured at fair value (primarily Level 2); accounting for economic hedges, fair value hedges (including excluded components to OCI), cash flow hedges (OCI to earnings), and net investment hedges (CTA in OCI); cash flows presented consistent with hedged items (see Note 9).
- Variable Interest Entities: introduction to VIE concept (entities lacking sufficient equity or with limited decision-making by equity holders), with details continuing beyond the excerpt.

nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.20 Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The functional currency of our foreign operations is generally the local currency.
nodes.summary:
- Uncertain tax positions: Uses a two-step process—recognition (more-likely-than-not threshold assuming full examination by tax authorities) and measurement (largest benefit >50% likely upon settlement). Differences between returns and financial statement recognition affect taxes payable/refundable and deferred taxes. Significant judgment impacts the effective tax rate.
- Stock-based compensation: Recognized for employees and directors based on estimated fair value of awards.
- Foreign currency: Local currency is generally the functional currency; income statement translated at average rates, assets/liabilities at period-end rates. Translation adjustments recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss; transaction gains/losses recorded in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Pension and postretirement costs accrued for service and interest; prior service costs/credits amortized; expected return based on fair value of assets. Actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net in the year incurred; plans measured annually (Dec 31) or upon remeasurement. Management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy service. Funded status recognized on the balance sheet; certain items recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss), net of tax.
- Derivative instruments: Used to manage FX and interest rate risk (e.g., swaps, caps, forwards); not for trading. Measured at fair value (primarily Level 2). Economic hedge changes recognized in current earnings. Fair value hedge changes recorded in earnings for both derivative and hedged item; excluded components to OCI and amortized. Cash flow hedge changes to OCI and reclassified when hedged items affect earnings. Net investment hedge changes recorded in OCI as part of CTA. Derivative cash flows classified consistent with hedged items.
- Variable interest entities (VIEs): Introduction of criteria indicating entities that lack sufficient equity or decision-making power (section truncated).

nodes.title: Employee Benefit Plans
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.21 Employee Benefit Plans
nodes.start_phrase: Pension and postretirement health care and life insurance benefits earned during the year, as well as interest on projected benefit obligations, are accrued.
nodes.summary:
- Uncertain tax positions: Applies a two-step ASC 740 process—recognition (more-likely-than-not standard presuming full examination) and measurement (largest benefit with >50% likelihood). Differences from tax returns can affect current taxes payable/refunds and deferred tax assets/liabilities. Significant judgment impacts the effective tax rate.

- Stock-based compensation: Measures and recognizes expense for employee and director awards at estimated fair value (see Note 10).

- Foreign currency: Foreign operations generally use local functional currency. Translates income statements at average rates and balance sheets at period-end rates; translation adjustments recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive loss; transaction gains/losses in Other income (expense), net.

- Employee benefit plans: Accrues pension and postretirement service and interest costs; amortizes prior service costs/credits; expected return based on assumed return applied to fair value of assets; actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net in the period incurred; measured annually at Dec 31 or upon remeasurement. Management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy service. Recognizes funded status on the balance sheet; prior service amounts recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive income (loss), net of tax (see Note 11).

- Derivative instruments: Uses derivatives (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps, caps, swaptions, FX forwards) to manage FX and interest rate risk, not for trading. All derivatives are at fair value (primarily Level 2) on the balance sheet. Accounting by hedge type: economic hedges to current earnings; fair value hedges—both derivative and hedged item changes in earnings with excluded components in OCI and amortized; cash flow hedges—changes in OCI and reclassified when the hedged item affects earnings; net investment hedges—changes in OCI within cumulative translation adjustment. Cash flows align with the classification of hedged items (see Note 9).

- Variable interest entities: Begins defining VIEs as entities with insufficient equity or equity investors lacking decision-making power; section is truncated.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.22 Derivative Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: We enter into derivative transactions primarily to manage our exposure to fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates and interest rates.
nodes.summary:
- Uncertain tax positions: Uses a two-step model—recognition (more-likely-than-not standard assuming full-information examination) and measurement (largest benefit >50% likely upon settlement). Differences between return positions and financial statement recognition affect taxes payable/refunds and deferred tax assets/liabilities. Significant judgment impacts the effective tax rate.
- Stock-based compensation: Measures and recognizes expense for employee and director awards at estimated fair value (see Note 10).
- Foreign currency: Local currency is generally the functional currency; translates income statements at average rates and balance sheets at period-end rates. Translation adjustments recorded in Accumulated other comprehensive loss; transaction gains/losses recorded in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefit plans: Accrues pension and postretirement service cost earned and interest on obligations; amortizes prior service costs/credits; expected return based on assumptions applied to fair value of assets. Recognizes actuarial gains/losses immediately in Other income (expense), measured annually at December 31 or upon remeasurement. Management employees no longer accrue pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy. Funded status recognized on the balance sheet; certain items recorded in AOCI net of tax (see Note 11).
- Derivative instruments and hedging: Uses derivatives (e.g., cross-currency swaps, interest rate swaps, caps, swaptions, FX forwards, treasury locks) for FX and interest rate risk management, not trading. Measures all derivatives at fair value (primarily Level 2). Accounting: economic hedges recognized in earnings; fair value hedges record changes in both derivative and hedged item in earnings with excluded components to OCI and amortized; cash flow hedges to OCI then reclassified to earnings; net investment hedges to OCI as part of CTA. Derivative cash flows classified consistently with hedged items (see Note 9).
- Variable Interest Entities: Introduces VIEs as entities lacking sufficient equity or whose equity holders lack decision-making power; section leads into consolidation considerations (text incomplete).

nodes.title: Variable Interest Entities
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.23 Variable Interest Entities
nodes.start_phrase: VIEs are entities that lack sufficient equity to permit the entity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support from other parties, have equity investors that do not have the ability to make significant decisions relating to the entity’s operations through voting rights, do not have the obligation to absorb the expected losses, or do not have the right to receive the residual returns of the entity.
nodes.summary:
- Uncertain tax positions: Two-step process under ASC 740—recognition based on a more-likely-than-not threshold assuming full examination, and measurement at the largest benefit >50% likely upon settlement. Differences versus tax returns can affect current taxes payable/receivable and deferred taxes. Significant judgment affects the effective tax rate.
- Stock-based compensation: Expense measured and recognized at grant-date fair value for employee and director awards (see Note 10).
- Foreign currency: Local currencies as functional; translate income statement at average rates and balance sheet at period-end rates; translation adjustments to Accumulated other comprehensive loss; transaction gains/losses in Other income (expense), net.
- Employee benefits: Pension and postretirement costs accrued for service and interest; prior service costs/credits amortized; expected return based on fair value of plan assets; actuarial gains/losses recognized in Other income (expense), net upon measurement; funded status recognized on balance sheet; related OCI, net of tax; Verizon management no longer accrues pension benefits or retiree medical subsidy (see Note 11).
- Derivatives and hedging: Used to manage FX and interest rate risk (e.g., swaps, caps, forwards); measured at fair value (primarily Level 2). Accounting by hedge type—economic hedges to current earnings; fair value hedges recognize derivative and hedged item changes in earnings with excluded components to OCI; cash flow hedges to OCI then to earnings; net investment hedges to OCI (CTA). Cash flows classified consistent with hedged items (see Note 9).
- Variable Interest Entities: Consolidate VIEs when the company is the primary beneficiary (power over significant activities and exposure to significant benefits/losses).
- Recently adopted standards: Adopted ASU 2016-13 (CECL) on January 1, 2020 via modified retrospective approach; reduced retained earnings by $200 million (see Note 8).
- Revenue and contract costs (Note 2): Revenue from telecom services and wireless equipment; reported by Consumer and Business segments, with Corporate and other including captive insurance and divested operations. Certain revenues outside Topic 606 (leases, captive reinsurance, interest on device financing via agents); elected practical expedient to combine lease/non-lease components for some customer premise equipment; non-Topic 606 revenues of ~$3.2B (2022), $3.1B (2021), $2.9B (2020).
- Remaining performance obligations: Applies practical expedient to exclude contracts with original duration ≤1 year; substantial use of month-to-month contracts—approx. 94% of wireless postpaid and 92% of wireline Consumer/SMB at 12/31/22 (vs. 93% and 86% at 12/31/21). Options for add-on services recognized when exercised. Non-month-to-month contracts typically span >1 to up to 36 months (device plans) or up to 24 months (fixed-term). Usage-based/optional charges excluded from transaction price. Consumer includes wholesale reseller arrangements with stated terms.

nodes.title: Recently Adopted Accounting Standards
nodes.heading: 1.8.1.24 Recently Adopted Accounting Standards
nodes.start_phrase: On January 1, 2020, we adopted ASU 2016-13, Financial Instruments - Credit Losses (Topic 326) using the modified retrospective approach.
nodes.summary:
- Consolidation policy for variable interest entities (VIEs): the company consolidates VIEs when it is the primary beneficiary—i.e., it has the power to make key economic decisions and the obligation to absorb significant losses or the right to receive significant benefits.
- Adoption of ASU 2016-13 (CECL) on January 1, 2020 using a modified retrospective approach, resulting in a $200 million after-tax reduction to retained earnings; additional credit loss disclosures referenced in Note 8.
- Revenue recognition (Note 2): revenues arise primarily from telecommunications services and wireless equipment sales; reported by two segments—Consumer and Business—with Corporate and other including captive insurance revenues and historical results of divested businesses (e.g., Verizon Media).
- Non-ASC 606 revenues include leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on equipment financed via authorized agents; practical expedient under ASC 842 to combine lease and non-lease components for certain customer premise equipment; non-ASC 606 revenues were approximately $3.2B (2022), $3.1B (2021), and $2.9B (2020).
- Remaining performance obligations: uses the ASC 606 practical expedient to exclude contracts with original terms of one year or less. As of December 31, 2022, month-to-month contracts represented ~94% of wireless postpaid and ~92% of wireline Consumer and Small/Medium Business contracts (vs. ~93% and ~86% at December 31, 2021).
- Contract structures: services may be month-to-month (cancellable), up to 36 months under device payment plans, or up to 24 months under fixed-term plans; usage-based and optional add-on services are recognized when incurred and generally excluded from the transaction price.
- Consumer customers also include traditional wholesale resellers that purchase and resell wireless service under their own brands under stated-term arrangements.

nodes.title: Note 2. Revenue and Contract Costs
nodes.heading: 1.8.2 Note 2. Revenue and Contract Costs
nodes.start_phrase: We earn revenue from contracts with customers, primarily through the provision of telecommunications and other services and through the sale of wireless equipment.
nodes.summary:
- Explains consolidation policy for variable interest entities (VIEs), including how the primary beneficiary is identified (power over significant activities and exposure to significant benefits or losses).
- Discloses adoption of ASU 2016-13 (CECL) on January 1, 2020 using a modified retrospective approach, with a $200 million after-tax reduction to retained earnings; references further credit loss disclosures in Note 8.
- Outlines revenue recognition under Topic 606 for telecommunications services and wireless equipment sales, with disaggregation by two reportable segments (Consumer and Business); notes that “Corporate and other” includes captive insurance and results of divested businesses such as Verizon Media.
- Identifies revenues not accounted for under Topic 606, including leasing (towers and equipment), captive reinsurance for device insurance, and interest on equipment financed via device payment plans sold by authorized agents; notes use of a Topic 842 practical expedient to combine lease and non-lease components for certain customer premise equipment; provides amounts of non-Topic 606 revenues: $3.2B (2022), $3.1B (2021), $2.9B (2020).
- Describes remaining performance obligations and use of Topic 606 practical expedient to exclude contracts with original expected duration of one year or less; highlights prevalence of month-to-month contracts: approximately 94% of wireless postpaid and 92% of wireline Consumer/SMB at December 31, 2022 (vs. 93% and 86% at December 31, 2021).
- Details typical contract structures: month-to-month arrangements; device payment plans with terms up to 36 months; fixed-term plans up to 24 months; variable usage and optional add-on services recognized when incurred and generally excluded from transaction price due to cancelability; allocation of transaction price to unsatisfied service obligations mainly applies to non–month-to-month contracts.

nodes.title: Note 2. Revenue and Contract Costs - Introduction
nodes.heading: 1.8.2 Note 2. Revenue and Contract Costs
nodes.start_phrase: We earn revenue from contracts with customers, primarily through the provision of telecommunications and other services and through the sale of wireless equipment.
nodes.summary:
Note 2. Revenue and Contract Costs 
We earn revenue from contracts with customers, primarily through the provision of telecommunications and other services and through the sale of wireless equipment.

nodes.title: Revenue by Category
nodes.heading: 1.8.2.1 Revenue by Category
nodes.start_phrase: We have two reportable segments that we operate and manage as strategic business units, Consumer and Business.
nodes.summary:
- Consolidation policy for variable interest entities (VIEs): the company consolidates VIEs when it is the primary beneficiary—i.e., it has the power to make key decisions affecting performance and has the obligation to absorb losses or the right to receive significant benefits.
- Recently adopted accounting standards: implemented ASU 2016-13 (CECL, Topic 326) on January 1, 2020 via a modified retrospective approach, decreasing retained earnings by $200 million (from $53,147 million to $52,947 million); additional credit loss disclosures referenced in Note 8.
- Revenue recognition overview: revenue from contracts with customers for telecommunications and other services and wireless equipment; two reportable segments (Consumer and Business). Corporate and other includes captive insurance revenues and historical results of divested businesses (e.g., Verizon Media).
- Non-Topic 606 revenues: include leasing (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance for wireless device insurance, and interest on equipment financed through authorized agents. The company applies a Topic 842 practical expedient to combine lease and non-lease components for certain customer-premise equipment. Amounts were approximately $3.2B (2022), $3.1B (2021), and $2.9B (2020).
- Remaining performance obligations: uses the Topic 606 practical expedient to exclude contracts with original durations of one year or less (primarily month-to-month). As of December 31, 2022, month-to-month contracts comprised ~94% of wireless postpaid and ~92% of wireline Consumer/SMB (vs. ~93% and ~86% at December 31, 2021).
- Options for additional services: fees recognized when customers exercise the options, typically month-to-month.
- Wireless contract structures: include month-to-month cancellable arrangements; device payment plans with terms up to 36 months; and fixed-term plans up to 24 months. Usage-based and optional add-on charges are excluded from the transaction price.
- Allocation of transaction price: unsatisfied or partially satisfied service performance obligations primarily relate to non–month-to-month contracts.
- Consumer channel also serves traditional wholesale resellers that purchase and resell wireless service under their own brands under stated-term arrangements.

nodes.title: Remaining Performance Obligations
nodes.heading: 1.8.2.2 Remaining Performance Obligations
nodes.start_phrase: When allocating the total contract transaction price to identified performance obligations, a portion of the total transaction price may relate to service performance obligations which were not satisfied or are partially satisfied as of the end of the reporting period.
nodes.summary:
- Consolidation policy for variable interest entities (VIEs): Verizon consolidates VIEs when it is the primary beneficiary—i.e., it has the power to make key economic decisions and the obligation to absorb significant losses or right to significant benefits.
- Recently adopted accounting standard: Implemented ASU 2016-13 (Topic 326) on January 1, 2020 using the modified retrospective approach; reduced retained earnings by $200 million (from $53,147 million to $52,947 million).
- Revenue recognition overview (Topic 606): Revenue primarily from telecom services and wireless equipment; reported by two segments (Consumer and Business). Corporate and other includes captive insurance and historical results of divested businesses (e.g., Verizon Media).
- Non-Topic 606 revenues: From leases (towers/equipment), captive reinsurance, and interest on agent-financed equipment; totaled approximately $3.2B (2022), $3.1B (2021), and $2.9B (2020).
- Remaining performance obligations (RPO) and practical expedients:
  - Excludes contracts with original expected duration of one year or less.
  - High prevalence of month-to-month contracts: at 12/31/22, ~94% of wireless postpaid and 92% of wireline Consumer/SMB; at 12/31/21, ~93% wireless postpaid and 86% wireline Consumer/SMB.
  - Wireless contracts may be month-to-month, up to 36 months (device payment plans), or up to 24 months (fixed-term); usage-based and optional services recognized when incurred.
  - Reseller (wholesale) contracts can exceed two years and may include minimum revenue commitments.
  - Business wireline contracts often 12 months or less; some longer with fixed and usage fees; certain wireline/telematics contracts include total-term minimum fees totaling $1.6B through April 2032 (excluded from time-band disclosures).
  - RPO expected recognition: $22.1B in 2023, $14.3B in 2024, and $8.1B thereafter; subject to change from modifications/terminations.
- Accounts receivable and contract balances:
  - Receivables from contracts with customers: $11,274M (2022), $10,758M (2021), $12,029M (Jan 1, 2021).
  - Device payment plan receivables: $16,648M (2022), $12,888M (2021), $10,358M (Jan 1, 2021).
  - Contract assets: $863M (2022), $934M (2021), $937M (Jan 1, 2021); arise mainly from equipment revenue recognized upfront under fixed-term plans; reclassified to A/R as services are billed; allowance for credit losses recorded at inception; balances remained relatively flat.
  - Contract liabilities: $8,234M (2022), $7,229M (2021), $5,598M (Jan 1, 2021); primarily advance billings for services; increases driven by sales promotions recognized over time and upfront fees (up $1.0B in 2022; up $1.6B in 2021).

nodes.title: Accounts Receivable and Contract Balances
nodes.heading: 1.8.2.3 Accounts Receivable and Contract Balances
nodes.start_phrase: The timing of revenue recognition may differ from the time of billing to our customers.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the nature and terms of Verizon’s customer contracts under ASC 606, distinguishing Consumer and Business arrangements for wireless, wireline, and telematics services. Consumer wireline is generally month-to-month, with some up to two-year terms; Business wireline contracts often include fixed monthly and usage-based fees, annual or total-term commitments, and in some cases contractual minimum fees.
- Notes certain Business wireline and telematics contracts with minimum fees totaling $1.6 billion through April 2032 are excluded from timing disclosure because revenue recognition timing cannot be predicted.
- Provides remaining performance obligations (RPO) at December 31, 2022: $22.1 billion expected in 2023, $14.3 billion in 2024, and $8.1 billion thereafter, subject to change from modifications or terminations.
- Explains the distinction between receivables (unconditional rights to consideration) and contract balances (assets/liabilities arising from timing differences between performance and cash collection).
- Reports balances at December 31, 2022: receivables of $11.3 billion and device payment plan receivables of $16.6 billion; exclusions include leasing, captive reinsurance, and certain agent-financed interest and sales.
- Presents contract assets of $863 million (classified in Prepaid expenses and other and Other assets) and contract liabilities of $8.234 billion (in Other current liabilities and Other liabilities); contract assets remained relatively flat in 2022 and 2021.
- Explains contract assets creation under fixed-term plans due to allocation between equipment and service, reclassified to accounts receivable as services are billed; credit loss allowances are recognized at inception and reassessed quarterly.
- Details contract liabilities primarily from advance service billings; increases of $1.0 billion in 2022 and $1.6 billion in 2021 driven by sales promotions recognized over time, upfront fees, and (in 2021) advanced billings and the TracFone acquisition; decreases from satisfaction of performance obligations and the Verizon Media sale. Revenue recognized from beginning contract liabilities was $5.0 billion in 2022 and $4.3 billion in 2021.
- Outlines capitalization of incremental costs to obtain contracts (commissions) and certain fulfillment costs (e.g., wireline circuit installation) when recoverable, with amortization ratably over expected benefit periods. Wireless acquisition costs are amortized over device upgrade cycles; Consumer wireline over the customer relationship period; Business wireline incremental costs are insignificant.
- States deferred contract costs are amortized over two to six years and assessed for impairment quarterly; impairment is recognized if carrying amount exceeds expected consideration less directly related costs.
- Reports deferred contract costs at December 31, 2022 of $5.104 billion ($2.629 billion current; $2.475 billion noncurrent) and amortization expense of $3.0 billion in both 2022 and 2021.

nodes.title: Contract Costs
nodes.heading: 1.8.2.4 Contract Costs
nodes.start_phrase: As discussed in Note 1, Topic 606 requires the recognition of an asset for incremental costs to obtain a customer contract, which are then amortized to expense over the respective periods of expected benefit.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue recognition and contract balances: Revenue recognized over time and from upfront fees; increases in deferred revenue from advanced billings and the TracFone acquisition, partially offset by satisfying performance obligations for wireless and Fios services and the sale of Verizon Media. $5.0B (2022) and $4.3B (2021) of revenue recognized from beginning-of-year contract liabilities. Contract assets were $863M at 12/31/22 (down from $934M), and contract liabilities were $8.234B at 12/31/22 (up from $7.229B).
